cells.tense: You are here, taking care of what's growing, and you're doing it with your own hands.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've tended that's close to done, and let yourself feel finished with it — completion opening the next thing rather than costing you something. Name it today.
cells.core:
You're tending what matters — the work, the people, the thing that's slowly taking shape — and you're doing it without forcing it or holding too tight. That's the balance point: care that doesn't exhaust, keeping hold without clutching. This is the good version, and you know it because things are actually growing while you do it.

That steadiness is free to feed something now. When one thing finishes, let it be finished — the ending isn't a loss, it's what lets the next thing start. Say out loud what you've brought to completion, and let the completion itself be the reward.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what's growing without forcing it — and it's working.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the part of you that moves through uncertainty with only enough light for the next step

cells.tense: You're already living in a future that isn't here yet, bracing for what it will need.
cells.ask: Let one thing that hasn't asked for you yet stay unwritten. Give your hands back to what's in front of you, and let what you've already imagined be enough for today.
cells.core:
You're caring for things ahead of time. Before a need arrives, you've already pictured it, and you're already arranging around it — holding space for what might not even be yours to hold. The care is real. But all of it is going out to loads that haven't landed, and it pulls you away from what's actually here.

What's worth trusting is what you've already lived through and absorbed — when you've fully taken something in, the vision of what comes next flows from it naturally, without the bracing. Give the future permission to stay open. There's satisfaction in what you've already imagined, and it doesn't need you to pre-build it.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding space for what hasn't arrived, and it's wearing you out.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the part of you that moves through uncertainty with only enough light for the next step

cells.tense: You're standing at a door you already walked past, and you haven't turned back toward the room.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing worth hoping for and follow it past the point where you usually stop. Let what you've cared for keep growing, and let it be seen when it does.
cells.core:
When this is going well here, you can move through fog without needing the whole road. You take one step on partial light, then the next one shows itself, and the not-knowing doesn't stop you tending what you've got your hands on. That capacity is still in you — you know how to care for what grows. But it's gone quiet, and you've stepped away from the unclear place where it used to work.

You didn't lose the ability to do it. You stopped turning up where it's needed. Underneath the quiet, the wanting is still there — the thing you cared about, the reason any of it mattered. Follow that wanting a little further than you normally would. When what you've been growing finally gets there, you'll know it by how brightly it shows.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to tend things. You've just stopped showing up to do it.

cells.tense: You're already moving through the ambiguity, already tending what's growing, but the way you tell it, it sounds like something happening to you.
cells.ask: Say 'this is mine' about one place where your care is the reason something is still growing. Say it once, today.
cells.core:
You're navigating uncertainty right now — feeling your way through, adjusting, tending what needs tending — and you keep describing it as if the situation were handling itself. Your hand is on it. You're the one showing up to the unclear thing and keeping hold of it. That's not something that's happening to you; it's something you're doing.

Your words haven't caught up with your hands. So claim one thing — one place where your tending is the reason something is still growing — and say it out loud. Not a whole life story. One thing. The care and attention that brought it this far is yours.
